# The Easy Method

> "Don't be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind."
>
> — Romans 12:2

This book has one aim: to change the way you think about masturbation.

That's all. It won't make you stronger, and it won't make you more disciplined. It will change what you see when you look at the habit, and once you see it clearly, stopping is easy.

One man had a girlfriend he was happy with and still couldn't leave the habit alone. Someone on a recovery forum pointed him to EasyPeasy, and he came back having understood the whole method in a single line: it works, he wrote, "because its all in the mind".

The usual way of quitting begins at the foot of a mountain. You stare up at it, take a deep breath, and spend the following weeks dragging yourself uphill, craving and feeling robbed. This way begins somewhere else entirely. You begin with relief, like a man walking out of the doctor's office with the all-clear. And the feeling doesn't fade. Years from now you'll look back at this stretch of your life and scratch your head over why you ever did it. When you meet men who are still stuck, you'll feel sorry for them. You won't envy them for a second.

## The instruction nobody likes {-}

Until you've finished the whole book, carry on as normal.

Don't start a streak. Don't make a vow. Don't cut down to weekends. Live exactly as you've been living.

Of all the instructions in this book, this is the one that gets the most complaints, and from Christian readers most of all. "You've just told me it's a sin, and now you're telling me to keep going?"

No. Nobody is ordering you to do anything. The instruction is this: don't launch a willpower campaign halfway through a book that is about to make willpower unnecessary. You've already tried it that way, probably dozens of times. A few more days of living as you are won't make you any worse, and they will let you do something you've never done before: watch the habit with your eyes open while the book explains what you're looking at. As you read, the wish to do it will shrink without any effort from you. Let it.

There's one exception. If you've already stopped, or you're a few days or weeks into a break and don't quite know what to call yourself, don't start again for the book's sake. Stay as you are. In truth you're already free, and the remaining chapters will simply let your head catch up with your hands.

By the way, there's no "one last time" ceremony waiting for you in the closing pages. The final step of this book is a prayer, and you'll be glad to pray it.

## What have you got to lose? {-}

Some men never finish this book. They feel a loss coming, so they stall. A few ration themselves to a paragraph a day, like a boy eating his vegetables one pea at a time.

Look at it coldly. Suppose you read every page and nothing changes. Then you've lost a few hours, and you're exactly where you are today. Suppose instead it works. Then you've got your life back. Blaise Pascal, a Christian and a very sharp mathematician, would have recognised the bet: nothing to lose on one side, everything to gain on the other. Only a fool turns that down.

## Why the normal way is so hard {-}

The normal way of quitting goes like this. You write down everything the habit costs you: the guilt, the tiredness, the lost time, the distance from God. Then you tell yourself:

"If I can just hold out long enough, the urge will finally die, and then I'll be happy."

It sounds sensible. Men do get free this way. But it is the hard road, and most men who take it end up where this man did:

> "anything that required 'human effort' ultimately failed me at some point or other"
>
> — a man on a Christian forum

Or this one, who threw everything he had at it:

> "I tried fasting, abstaining, and reading my Bible, yet every time it returned, stronger than before."
>
> — a 43-year-old man, in a testimony on a Christian site

Here is why it's so hard.

**1. Stopping was never the problem.** You stop every single time you finish. In that flat, grey minute afterwards, you are the most committed quitter on earth. "Never again. I mean it this time." Every man says it, and every man means it. The problem is not that minute. The problem is day three, or day thirty, or day three hundred, when you're tired or lonely and a quiet voice says "just this once". One becomes two, and you're back where you started, minus a little more self-respect. For some men it doesn't even take until day three. A nineteen-year-old, raised in a strict Christian home, wrote about his first time: "I vowed never to do that again, only to find myself searching for a secret place after a couple of hours."

**2. Guilt and fear make you reach for it.** What does a man do when he feels ashamed, anxious and worthless? He looks for comfort. And what has he trained himself to use for comfort? Tell a man the habit is ruining him and you've just handed him one more reason to escape into it tonight. A counsellor on a Christian recovery blog saw it clearly: "Shame is the problem for so many, many Christians." This is why the scare videos and the thundering sermons have never freed you. They load the gun.

**3. Every reason to stop makes stopping harder.** That sounds mad, so take it slowly. First, your reasons tell you that you *ought* to give something up, which means part of you goes on believing there is something to give up: a comfort, a treat, an old friend. You feel like a man being marched away from his only pleasure. Second, your reasons point your eyes at the wrong question. You don't do it because of the reasons you should stop. Nobody jerks off *because* it leaves him flat and guilty. The real question is the other one: why do you want to do it at all?

The same forum man spotted the trap inside all that effort: "The more you try and try and try to stop thinking about porn, the more you keep making it the center of your thoughts". Swap in the word "masturbation" and nothing changes.

Even the hard men of the internet have noticed. One coach has built a whole channel on discipline, and his advice on vices comes down to five words: "Do not rely on willpower."

## Three questions {-}

So for now we're going to put your reasons for stopping on a shelf. All of them, including the good ones, including the godly ones. We'll come back for them.

In their place, look straight at the habit and ask:

1. **What is it actually doing for me?**
2. **Do I actually enjoy it?**
3. **Why am I doing this to myself?**

Here is the beautiful truth, and the rest of the book exists to prove it to you: masturbation does nothing for you. NOTHING.

Be clear about what that means. I'm not saying the costs are bigger than the benefits. Every man already knows that, and it has never helped him. I'm saying there are no benefits. Not one. The relaxation, the sleep, the stress relief, the "release": each of them is an illusion, and we'll take them apart one at a time.

Most men feel obliged to explain why they do it. Listen to the explanations and you'll notice they're all excuses, and that the men giving them don't sound convinced.

This is what Paul meant by "the renewing of your mind". He didn't say to try harder. He said to be transformed by seeing things differently. If you're an atheist, play along: call it changing your mind, which is the only thing that has ever changed a man.

## What happens next {-}

First we clear away the illusions. As they fall, you'll discover that you're not being asked to give up anything at all.

Then, once the feeling of sacrifice is gone, and you know that life without the habit is not just bearable but far better, we'll take your reasons back down off the shelf. The energy. The time. The clean conscience. Looking your wife, your friends and your God in the eye. We'll even suggest an experiment or two for the first weeks that many men swear by.

By then those reasons won't be a stick to beat yourself with. They'll be the bonus on top of the thing you really wanted from the start: to be a free man, master of yourself, with nothing to hide.
